name: Shrinkhala Devi Shakti Peetha, Pandua
deity: The Goddess as Shrinkhala Devi, the Goddess of the Chain, a Shakti Peetha of Sati
period: Named in the stotram ascribed to Adi Shankara (8th century) as the seat at Pradyumna; the shrine itself is lost or disputed, and the site is now marked by medieval Indo-Islamic monuments
dynasty: Traditional Shakta seat; later Bengal Sultanate-era monuments on the site
style: Bengal (no standing temple; the site is marked by an Indo-Islamic minar and mosque)
summary: Named in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha Stotram as Pradyumne Shrinkhala Devi, the Goddess of the Chain is remembered at Pandua in Hooghly, where Sati's stomach is said to have fallen, a seat whose exact shrine is debated and no longer stands.

sections.history: Shrinkhala Devi appears in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha Stotram, ascribed to Adi Shankara, in the line Pradyumne Shrinkhala Devi, the Goddess of the Chain at Pradyumna. Local tradition identifies this Pradyumna with Pandua, a town in Hooghly district of West Bengal, though the identification is not universal: some lists place the seat elsewhere, and a second Pandua lies in Malda district. The Pandua of Hooghly is known as a medieval town with a great minar and the ruins of a ruler's palace, and the site is today dominated by a tall brick tower and a mosque under the care of the Archaeological Survey of India. Accounts of the minar's origin conflict, as a thirteenth-century victory tower to some and a later monument to others, and some devotional accounts hold that it rose over or in place of the Goddess's older shrine. That cannot be established from the sources consulted. The honest position is that the seat is recalled by tradition rather than by a surviving temple.
sections.architecture: No temple of Shrinkhala Devi is known to stand at Pandua today. The monument that rises there is the Pandua Minar, an Indo-Islamic tower of about 38 metres, or 125 feet, set beside a mosque within a protected complex, and dated by different accounts to the thirteenth century or later. Devotees who come for the Goddess therefore find not a sanctum but an open ground of old brick, a tall silent tower and the memory of the place. The surrounding country is the flat alluvial plain of the Hooghly and Damodar basin.
sections.legends: In the Puranic story Sati, daughter of Daksha, gives up her life at her father's sacrifice after he insults Shiva. Shiva wanders the world carrying her body, and Vishnu's discus divides it so that its parts fall in sacred places, each afterwards worshipped as a Shakti Peetha. At Pradyumna it is her stomach that tradition says fell, and the Goddess there is Shrinkhala, a name meaning chain. The name of the Bhairava who guards the seat is not firmly recorded in the sources consulted. A further tale tells of the sage Rishyasringa, who circling the hill at Pandua in devotion felt the presence of the Goddess and, at her direction, travelled on to Sringeri in Karnataka, an echo that ties this Bengal seat to a southern tradition.
sections.festivals: Navaratri and Durga Puja, the great autumn worship of the Goddess in Bengal, is the season in which devotees most naturally remember this seat. No temple festival of Shrinkhala Devi has been verified at the site. A fair of about a month is reported each February in the grounds of the minar, attended by both Hindu and Muslim communities, but its link to the Goddess is not established. Confirm all dates locally.
sections.experience: Pandua is a place of memory more than of ritual. Reach it by local train from Howrah, then a short ride from the station to the minar, and walk the protected grounds in the quiet of the morning. Standing before the tower, a devotee may recall the stotram and the Goddess of the Chain in silence, and some pilgrims bring the line Pradyumne Shrinkhala Devi with them as a prayer. The ground is a shared and protected monument with a mosque beside it, so come as a considerate visitor and let the place be what it is today, an old seat of the Goddess remembered more by the heart than by stone.

visit.timings: As a protected monument the site is generally open in daylight hours, and there is no temple schedule of worship. Confirm current timings with the Archaeological Survey of India or locally before travelling.
visit.dressCode: Modest dress is advised, with shoulders and knees covered, as the grounds include a mosque. Remove footwear where asked and follow the posted rules.
visit.photography: Photography of the monument in the open grounds is generally allowed at protected sites, but follow posted signs, avoid photographing people at prayer, and ask before photographing anyone.
visit.gettingThere: Pandua, spelled Pundooah at its station, stands on the Howrah–Bardhaman main line in Hooghly district, some 60 km from Howrah and 50 km or so from Kolkata, which has the nearest major airport. The minar is a short toto or auto-rickshaw ride from the station. Do not confuse this town with Pandua in Malda district, which is a different place.
